# A one-third depth theorem for an actual integer-base interval centroid

Let C be a compact convex body in R x R. Suppose its positive-length
integer fibers are nonempty and its TRUE, unweighted mixed-length centroid
has integer base coordinate. Then that centroid is a single point of
S=C intersect (Z x R), and its normalized mixed-length halfspace depth
is strictly greater than 1/3.

This theorem allows any number of positive interval fibers and every
closed ambient halfspace. It is conditional on the actual integer-base
centroid hypothesis. It is not the all-n, all-d statement (OC).

## Dependencies

The following proved notes supply the exact finite lemmas used here:

1. `candidate ad8324f468564d7c`: the strict quadratic
   estimate Q>(2/3)mM and the centered slab-tail bound
   T_(>h),T_(<-h)>=[M-(2h+1)m]/3, with complete elementary proofs.
2. `candidate bca993ec81e97cb4`: finite nonvertical
   attainment and the exact nine-case endpoint analysis producing either
   no wholly captured fibers or a symmetric proper block with no endpoint
   coincidences. It handles the vertical boundary-fiber masses separately.

No unproved auxiliary lemma is used below.

## 1. Coordinates and the actual centroid

Zero-length fibers contribute no mixed length. Positive fibers have
consecutive integer indices, by convexity. The positive part of the mixed
measure has the same centroid and cap masses as the whole measure. Its
centroid belongs to C by convexity, and the assumed integer base therefore
puts it in S. Translate that base and its continuous coordinate to zero.
For a chosen nonvertical cap, a shear preserving the integer base, followed
if needed by reflection of the continuous coordinate, gives cap equation
x>=0 and fibers

    K_i=[l_i,r_i],   w_i=r_i-l_i>0,
    M=sum w_i,   Q=sum w_i^2,   m=max w_i.

The endpoints l are convex and r concave. The centroid equations are

    sum i w_i=0,   sum w_i r_i=Q/2.                  (2)

Their Jensen inequalities imply `l_0<0<r_0`, so the central fiber is proper.
Replacing C by the hull of its positive fibers does not change any positive
fiber or cap mass. The angular lemma applies to that hull; extra original
zero-length fibers do not affect its measured inequalities.

## 2. No wholly captured fiber

If the cap wholly captures none of the positive fibers, its mass is
`F=sum (r_i)_+`. Equation (2) and w_i<=m imply

    mF>=sum w_i(r_i)_+>=Q/2,
    F/M>=Q/(2mM)>1/3.                                (3)

Endpoint contacts at an upper endpoint have zero length and are included.

## 3. A symmetric proper block and a captured tail

The angular lemma reduces all remaining minimizing caps to the case where
the proper fibers are I={-h,...,h}, k=2h+1, with no endpoint contacts.
Each nonempty outer tail is entirely captured or entirely excluded; at
least one is captured. Let T be the total captured-tail mass. Then

    F=sum_(i in I)r_i+T.                             (4)

If km>=M and h>=1, let L_i=c+b i be the chord through r_-h and r_h.
Here c=(r_-h+r_h)/2>0. Put e_i=r_i-L_i. Concavity gives e_i>=0 on I
and e_i<=0 outside I. Since the weighted base mean is zero and the
unweighted sum of indices in I is zero, equation (2) yields

    Q/2=sum w_i r_i
       <=Mc+m sum_(i in I)e_i
       =m sum_(i in I)r_i+c(M-km)
       <=m sum_(i in I)r_i.

Thus (3) holds again. If h=0 and km>=M, positivity forces the single-fiber
case, whose centroid depth is 1/2; it has no captured-tail complication.

It remains to consider km<=M. The probability distribution w_i/M is
a mean-preserving spread of the uniform probability on I. To verify the
precise assertion, its signed difference from that uniform law is
nonpositive on I, nonnegative outside I, and has total and first moment
zero. For a convex function, subtract the chord joining its values at
-h and h. The resulting function is nonpositive inside and nonnegative
outside, so its integral against this signed difference is nonnegative.
This proves the convex-order inequality. When h=0 use Jensen directly.
Applying it to the concave sequence r in (2) gives

    sum_(i in I)r_i >= k Q/(2M)>km/3.               (5)

At least one tail is captured, so the scalar slab-tail theorem gives
`T>=[M-km]/3`. Combining with (4)--(5) gives F>M/3.

## 4. Every closed ambient halfspace

The angular lemma proves that the least mass among all containing closed
halfspaces is attained by a finite nonvertical cap of one of the two cases
above. Its proof moves containing halfspaces inward through the centroid,
uses continuous piecewise affine cap mass for finite slopes, and compares
vertical closed caps with finite plateaus while retaining the entire
central boundary fiber. Thus the strict bound for the attained least cap
proves the bound for every closed containing halfspace, including all
oblique slopes and vertical boundary mass.

The single positive-fiber case was treated directly. Other zero-length
fibers require no deletion from S and contribute zero to this full-length
measure. This statement makes no assertion about a purely atomic q=0
intersection or higher continuous or integer dimension.
